un-ga-res-448:
News from the Netherlands shapes Resolution 448, adopted by the General Assembly on 12 December 1950. The Dutch state wrote in June of that year with a change. It would no longer send facts on Indonesia to the UN under Article 73 of the Charter, save for West New Guinea. The reason was plain: the Republic of Indonesia now stood fully free, and had just joined the UN as a member.

The Assembly takes note of the Dutch letter with pleasure. It recalls its 1948 stand on two points. Growth of self-rule in lands not yet free is welcome. And the UN must be told when a land's status changes so much that reports are no longer owed. A short set of requests to its study team follows.
un-ga-res-48:
One more winter of want faced war-torn lands as the General Assembly passed Resolution 48 on 11 December 1946. The relief agency UNRRA was winding down. The Assembly notes that some states would need cash aid in 1947 to import food and other bare needs of life. World bodies and private aid, it fears, may not cover that need in full.

Where such aid fails to come, the text warns, hunger and suffering will follow through winter, spring, and early summer. The leftover relief need must be met at speed, and without waste or doubled effort. Member states had voiced their will to do their part. The vote is a bridge from wartime relief to the great aid plans of the years ahead.
un-ga-res-a-69-48:
Step by step is the path urged in Resolution A/69/48, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its subject is the cut of the nuclear threat by stages. The text recalls the first vote on the plan, in 1994, and the chain that has run each year since. It restates the world pledge: the total end of nuclear arms, and a world free of them for good.

Two older pacts are held up as guides on the road: the 1972 ban on germ arms, and the ban on chemical arms that came after it. Each shows, the text argues, that a whole class of arms can be wiped out by pact. The nuclear class, it holds, must meet the same end, by steps that can be checked.

Matthias Nahrendorf, Ralph Weissleder, and Georg Ertl asked in 2006 whether a clotting factor is needed for the heart to heal. After a myocardial infarction, a heart attack, the dead muscle is replaced by scar tissue. Factor XIII helps stabilize blood clots, and the team tested whether lacking it impairs wound healing in the heart.

The question links bleeding biology to recovery: a repair process that starts with a clot may falter if the clot is weak. Their title poses the question plainly, and the study answers it in the injured heart. arxiv-2606-05348: Probabilistic programs reason under uncertainty, but inference — computing the answers — is painfully slow when data arrives piece by piece. arxiv-2606-05448: Pumping CO2 underground for storage means tracking how fluids creep through porous rock — multiphase flow in porous media. arxiv-2606-05648: Asking for your nearest coffee shop can reveal where you are — k-nearest neighbor queries leak location. arxiv-2606-06248: Open star clusters shed tidal tails as they orbit the galaxy — and the Milky Way's bar bends those tails. arxiv-2606-06448: Long-horizon AI agents accumulate state — memories, plans, tool outputs — and systems buckle under it. tob-4148:
J. M. Rodwell's 1861 translation of the Koran was the first widely read English version made by a scholar who arranged the suras in what he judged chronological order. That innovation shaped Western study of the Quran for a century, letting readers trace the preaching's development from Meccan to Medinan periods. Rodwell's language is dated Victorian English.

His method, though, was pioneering, and his notes reflect serious engagement with Muslim tradition. Modern translators order the text traditionally and dispute some of Rodwell's judgments, but students of reception history still consult him. The volume stands as the Victorian doorway into Islam's scripture, learned, opinionated, and historically important.
tob-0148:
Farid ud-Din Attar, a Persian poet of the twelfth century, sent thirty birds on a quest in the Conference of the Birds. The hoopoe leads them across seven valleys to find the Simorgh, the king of birds. Most fall away; thirty reach the mountain at last.

There the pun at the poem's heart opens: si morgh, in Persian, means thirty birds. The seekers find themselves. Attar fills the road with tales of lovers, madmen, and saints that mirror each stage of the soul's path. The poem is Sufism's greatest allegory. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
podcast-dannyjones-QGCxNo5X348:
Julian Dorey hosts a wide-ranging interview podcast and joins Danny Jones, host to host, to discuss what he calls the deadliest conspiracy theory in the world. The two compare the claims that circulate through their shared world and settle on the one Dorey believes has killed the most people and done the deepest damage.

The conversation works as an industry summit: two men who interview everyone, believers and generals alike, comparing what they have heard off the record. Dorey's choice and his argument for it are the episode's payload, and listeners should treat the ranking as his judgment, not a measurement. The recording's interest is the peer-to-peer candor. Podcasters who usually ask the questions answer them here, and their map of which theories matter, and which merely entertain, differs from the audience's in instructive ways.
podcast-joerogan-Wi0nMTtLr48:
Boxing champion Terence Crawford visits Joe Rogan's MMA Show for number 145. Crawford had just beaten Errol Spence Jr. in a clash of unbeaten champions. Fans and judges had long denied him full credit.

Crawford says he always felt he was the man, long before others agreed. Rogan notes how hard it was to make the dream fight happen. They talk about control, pace, and the joy of finally getting his flowers. The episode lets a quiet champion explain his rise in his own calm words, with respect earned the hard way.
squier-davis-ancient-monuments-1848:
Surveyors with chains and compasses gave the mound debate its first hard facts in 1848. Ancient Monuments of the Mississippi Valley, by Ephraim Squier and Edwin Davis, was the first book the Smithsonian issued. The two men mapped and dug the great earthworks of Ohio and beyond.

Their plans and measures of forts, mounds, and sacred rings are exact and rich in detail. Claims about the builders could now be tested against drawn proof for the first time. Every later fight over the mounds cites this volume, for or against. It stands as the founding record of American field archaeology.
daedalus-sea-serpent-reports-1848:
A British warship met a sea serpent in the South Atlantic in 1848, and the report would not die. The Daedalus dossier in The Zoologist gathers Captain Peter M'Quhae's report to the Admiralty, Lieutenant Edgar Drummond's journal, and the Times prints of the tale. A like sighting from the ship Daphne stands in the file as well.

The officers told of a long neck, a mane, and a head held clear of the sea at close range. Their rank and calm tone made doubters pause, and the row ran for months in print. No sea serpent report of the age is half so famed. The dossier is the whole quarrel in one file.
bunsen-egypts-place-universal-history-vo:
Christian Bunsen set Egypt in the frame of all past time in Vol. 1 of Egypt's Place in Universal History, out in English in 1848. Bunsen was a man of state and a deep sage of tongues. Charles Cottrell turned his German text to English. This tome lays the base: sources, scripts, and the first dates for the kings.

His dates were bold and oft too long. Yet he taught English fans to ask when, not just what. The set runs to five fat tomes. This first one is its ground stone.
crowe-night-side-of-nature-1848:
Catherine Crowe made ghosts a grave theme in The Night-Side of Nature, her book of 1848. Crowe was a tale smith in Edinburgh. She felt that men of science scorned tales of shades for no good cause. She set out to hoard the best tales: shades at death beds, dreams that rang true, and houses no one could rest in.

Her calm, clear prose won a wide crowd. The book came just as the Fox raps crossed the sea. It primed the land to take the new faith to heart. It is a ground stone of ghost lore.
stearne-confirmation-discovery-witchcraf:
John Stearne backs his mate's hunt in A Confirmation and Discovery of Witchcraft, his book of 1648. Stearne worked by Matthew Hopkins in the great East Anglia hunt. Towns paid them to quiz, watch, and search the charged. Here Stearne prints the words of folk hanged since 1645, as proof the craft is real and the hunt was just in its harsh work.

He meets foes of the hunt point by point. His tone is prim, firm, and free of doubt. The book is the hunt's full case from its next chief hand. It is a hard read.
seidel-pneumatologia-1648:
Abraham Seidel sets out the lore of souls in Pneumatologia, his Latin work of 1648. The name means the study of spirits. Seidel was a church sage in the German lands in the midst of the great war that tore them. His book sorts the kinds of souls: angels, demons, the ghosts of the dead, and the strange forms that plague houses, fields, and the dreams of men in that torn age.

He weighs tales of marvels by the Good Book's rule. Wild claims get a strict sift. The text, in Latin, is a late sum of its school. It shows its age's fears.
sperling-de-magia-1648:
Johann Sperling set out ten short claims about magic in this Latin work, printed in 1648. It took the form of a school debate, held at the town of Wittenberg. Such debates let scholars test ideas in public, point by point.

The ten claims deal with magic and with demons, and what each one is said to do. Readers get a clear view of how a trained mind of that age sorted real acts from false ones. Short and plain, it shows the old schools at work on a dark theme.
barddas-iolo-morganwg-1848:
Iolo Morganwg was a Welsh poet and stone mason who claimed to have found old Bardic texts. This set came out after his death, in the 1862 and 1874 printings of his work. The editor J. Williams ab Ithel put the texts in print. Iolo said the lore came from the druids of old Wales.

In truth, much of the lore was Iolo's own work, shaped in his own mind. The texts set out gods, rites, and rules for bards in a neat scheme. False as old lore, the book still shaped the whole modern druid revival.
needham-observations-generation-1748:
John Turberville Needham, an English priest and man of science, read this paper to the Royal Society in 1748. He claimed to have seen life spring up where none had been. His claim dealt with the birth, make up, and break down of living stuffs. The theme drew heat, since it bore on how life first came to be on earth.

Needham boiled broth, sealed it, and found tiny forms in it days later. He took this as proof that dead stuff holds a force that makes new life. Pasteur and Spallanzani spent the next age of work to show where his trials went wrong.
poe-eureka-1848:
Edgar Allan Poe called Eureka a prose poem when it came out in 1848. He held it the great work of his life. The book sets out his view of how the cosmos was made and how it will end. Poe gave the core of it first as a talk in New York.

One prime burst, he holds, flung all stuff out through space. That stuff now draws back, grain to grain, to one mass once more. His view of a world that grows from one start struck fans as a flash of the Big Bang thought. The book is Poe's bold leap at the whole of things.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-8-1848:
Book Eight of the Antiquities of Mexico came out in 1848. Lord Kingsborough had died in debt in 1837, and the set had stalled for years. The full work runs to nine books in all. This book takes the long run of plates toward its close.

Texts and plates on the towns, gods, and past of old Mexico fill the book. The copies in the set save the look of books now lost or worn. Kingsborough's wild claim on the roots of the Mexicans drove the whole work. The set stands as a great store in spite of that claim.
kingsborough-mexico-vol-9-1848:
Book Nine ends Lord Kingsborough's Antiquities of Mexico. The last book came out in 1848, long past his death in 1837. The full set runs to nine books of plates and text. Kingsborough had spent his whole fortune on the work and died in a debt jail.

The last plates round out the store of codices and town views. Text in the set backs his claim that Mexico's folk came from the lost tribes. That claim has few friends now, but the plates endure. The set is a chief source for the art of old Mexico.
bronte-tenant-of-wildfell-hall-1848:
Anne Brontë published The Tenant of Wildfell Hall in 1848, under the name Acton Bell. The novel shocked readers with its tale of a wife fleeing a drunken, brutal husband. It is now read as a bold feminist work far ahead of its Victorian moment.

Helen Graham, a lone widow with a small son, rents Wildfell Hall and paints for bread. Village gossip paints her as fallen, and Gilbert Markham learns her tale from her diary. The diary tells of Arthur Huntingdon's charm, drink, and cruelty, and her flight to save her son. She nurses the dying Huntingdon yet will not return to his house of sin. Brontë insists a wife may save herself, a claim that drew fierce attacks then.
dumas-vicomte-de-bragelonne-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published The Vicomte de Bragelonne in serial form from 1847 to 1850 in France. The huge novel is the third and last of the d'Artagnan romances in his musketeer cycle. English editions often split it into parts, of which this volume is the first great slice.

Thirty-five years on, d'Artagnan serves the young Louis XIV as the crown seeks real power. Raoul, the vicomte and Athos's son, loves Louise de la Vallière, whom the king soon eyes. Court plots, English restoration schemes, and old friendships strain under the rising Sun King's ambition at court. The tone darkens as youth's fellowship gives way to age, rank, and royal will. Readers meet here the seeds of the iron mask tale that ends the saga.
dumas-ten-years-later-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published Ten Years Later as part of the Vicomte de Bragelonne cycle in France. English publishers split the vast final musketeer novel into titled parts for their readers in translation. This part presses on with Louis XIV's young court and the musketeers' last great acts together.

Raoul's hopeless love for Louise, now the king's mistress, drives him toward a soldier's death abroad. Aramis rises as a churchman with secret designs on the throne of France itself in time. Porthos, Athos, and d'Artagnan feel age and the new reign crowd out their old free world. Court balls and secret prisons frame a tale of friendship under a hardening absolute rule. The part builds toward the twin-prince plot that made the cycle's end so famous.
dumas-louise-de-la-valliere-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published Louise de la Vallière as part of the Vicomte de Bragelonne cycle in France. English editions carve this titled part from the vast final musketeer novel for separate sale in translation. Its center is the young Louis XIV's first great love and the court it remakes around him.

Louise, a maid of honor, loves the king in secret and with a pure, timid heart. Raoul, her betrothed and Athos's son, is sent away as the king clears his path to her. Madame de Montespan waits in the wings, and court ritual smothers private feeling with splendor. Aramis meanwhile learns a state secret that could shake the throne, the twin in prison. Dumas blends romance and high politics in the twilight of the musketeers' long service.
dumas-man-in-the-iron-mask-1848:
Alexandre Dumas published The Man in the Iron Mask as the close of the musketeer cycle. English editions print this famed part of the Vicomte de Bragelonne as a book by itself. Its plot turns on the legend of a masked prisoner, twin to Louis XIV of France.

Aramis plots to swap the king with his jailed twin and rule France through the double. Porthos dies in a cave blast, and Athos fades as his son Raoul seeks death abroad. D'Artagnan, torn between plot and duty, keeps faith with the crown he has served for decades. The four friends' ends give the gay saga a grave and moving final chord of loss. Few adventure cycles close with such weight on friendship, age, and passing time.
mill-principles-political-economy-vol-1-:
John Stuart Mill published Principles of Political Economy, Volume 1, in 1848. For fifty years the Principles served as the dominant textbook of economics in English. Volume 1 treats production: labor, capital, land, and the laws that govern their cooperation. Mill restates classical economics in a clear, final synthesis.

He studies large and small farming, cooperation, and the limits of growth in output. Mill writes with unusual care for the human side of industry. His sympathy for workers and for reform sets the book apart from colder texts. The stationary state, treated later, already casts its shadow. Volume 1 lays the base for the whole system.
mill-principles-political-economy-vol-2-:
John Stuart Mill completed Principles of Political Economy with Volume 2 in 1848. This volume treats distribution and exchange: wages, profits, rent, money, credit, and trade between nations. Mill argues that the laws of distribution are human-made and can be reformed. That claim opened economics to social reform.

He also develops the theory of value and of international trade in classic form. Chapters on the functions of government weigh taxes, education, and poor relief. Mill's hope for a stationary state of capital, paired with rising human culture, closes the work. The two volumes formed generations of economic thought. They remain readable and humane.
macaulay-history-england-vol-1-1848:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 1 of his History of England in 1848. The History became the best-selling work of history of the 1800s. Volume 1 opens with a survey of England from Roman times to the Restoration. It then focuses on the reign of Charles II and the accession of James II.

Macaulay writes Whig history: the story of liberty advancing through Parliament against kings. His famous third chapter paints the state of England in 1685 in rich detail. Markets, roads, alehouses, and clergy all come alive. The narrative art is brilliant and confident. Macaulay aimed to replace the novel in the reader's hands, and often succeeded.
macaulay-history-england-vol-2-1848:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 2 of his History of England in 1848, alongside the first. This volume covers the reign of James II in depth. James's push for Catholic power and standing armies alarms the nation. The trial of the Seven Bishops and the birth of a royal son spark crisis.

William of Orange lands in 1688, and James flees to France. Macaulay tells the road to revolution with narrative art at full power. His sympathies are clear: he honors those who defended law and Protestant liberty. Critics fault his partisanship, yet few deny his skill. The volume ends with William and Mary on the throne.
hume-enquiry-human-understanding-1748:
David Hume published An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1748 in London. Hume, a Scottish philosopher, recast the hard arguments of his earlier Treatise in a clearer, shorter form. The Enquiry became his most read statement of empiricism, the view that knowledge rests on experience.

Hume argued that we never see causes, only events following each other, yet the mind expects the pattern to hold. He tested miracles, free will, and belief in God against that standard and found them wanting. His calm, polite style carried radical doubts. The book still sets the terms for debates on reason, belief, and what the mind can know.
sydenham-works-vol1-1848:
Thomas Sydenham was a seventeenth-century English doctor famous for watching patients closely instead of trusting medical theory. Because he followed the example of Hippocrates, people called him the English Hippocrates. R. G. Latham translated his Latin works for the Sydenham Society, and this first volume came out in 1848.

The writings cover fevers and the great epidemics that swept through London in his lifetime. Sydenham sorted diseases by their steady symptoms, much as a botanist sorts plants by their form. He also recorded exact case notes and cures that he had tested at the bedside. His method helped start modern clinical medicine.
lowell-biglow-papers-1848:
James Russell Lowell published the first series of The Biglow Papers in 1848, during the Mexican-American War. Lowell, a young Massachusetts poet and abolitionist, wrote them as newspaper pieces in Yankee dialect. His farmer-poet Hosea Biglow speaks, while the learned Parson Wilbur adds mock-serious introductions.

Biglow's verses attack the war as a slaveholders' land grab and mock the politicians who sold it. A recruiting officer gets a famous dressing-down in rough, funny, perfectly rhymed dialect. Lowell based the speech on real New England talk, then sharpened it into a weapon. The papers became the masterpiece of American comic verse and the ancestor of all later dialect poetry in the United States.
lowell-fable-for-critics-1848:
James Russell Lowell published A Fable for Critics in 1848, the same year as The Biglow Papers made his name. Lowell was twenty-nine, brilliant, and unafraid of judging his elders. He cast the poem as a tour: the god Phoebus brings a visiting critic to meet America's living writers one by one.

Poe, Emerson, Hawthorne, Longfellow, Whittier, and Lowell himself each get a galloping verse portrait, praise and puncture mixed. Phoebus complains that American letters are all promise and brag. The judgments are so apt that many stuck to their subjects for life. The poem is the founding document of American critical reputation-making, and still the liveliest survey of the era's literature.
lowell-vision-sir-launfal-1848:
James Russell Lowell published The Vision of Sir Launfal in 1848, his telling of the Grail quest as a moral allegory. Lowell was in his great early burst, issuing the Biglow Papers and A Fable for Critics the same year. The poem's prelude, The Present Crisis, outgrew the poem itself in fame.

Sir Launfal rides out from his castle in pride, searching the world for the Holy Grail. He returns old and broken, and finds the Grail's lesson at his own gate, in sharing his last crust with a beggar. The Present Crisis, written against slavery's expansion, gave abolitionism a battle cry: truth forever on the scaffold, wrong forever on the throne. Generations of reformers quoted it, and Launfal's winter and summer landscapes remain lovely.
fichte-vocation-man-1848:
The Vocation of Man, Johann Gottlieb Fichte's Die Bestimmung des Menschen of 1800, is his most widely read book. William Smith's English translation of 1848, the first in the language, is the text here. Fichte wrote it for readers beyond the schools, in dialogue form, as a journey of one mind through its own doubts.

Doubt speaks first, stripping the world to a show of images. Knowledge answers, showing the mind its own laws at work in that show. Faith speaks last, and carries the speaker to duty, freedom, and trust in a moral order. The three voices move like acts in a play. No other work of Fichte's reaches the heart so directly.
rhazes-smallpox-measles-greenhill-1848:
The Persian doctor Rhazes, known in Arabic as al-Razi, wrote on smallpox and measles around the year 910. William Alexander Greenhill translated his treatise into English for the Sydenham Society in 1848. Rhazes was the first clinician to set the two diseases clearly apart. Generations of doctors had mixed their fevers and rashes together.

He describes each illness day by day: fever, pains, and the rising of the spots. Treatment follows his wide experience in Baghdad's hospitals. The work shows medieval Islamic medicine at its most observant. Its distinction between the diseases held for centuries. The translation made a classic of Eastern medicine open to English readers.
zoist-vol-06-1848:
March 1848 to January 1849 makes up the sixth volume of The Zoist. Europe's year of revolutions forms the backdrop to Elliotson's steady journal. Mesmeric cases arrive as usual: painless dentistry, cured fits, and sleeping subjects who seem to see afar. Cerebral physiology holds its share of the pages.

The journal's network of provincial doctors keeps the reports flowing. Elliotson, long expelled from polite medical society, edits with undimmed fight. Thirteen volumes from 1843 to 1856 form the movement's complete record. Volume six sits near the middle of that run. It shows mesmerism surviving scandal and fashion alike. The archive grows by accumulation.
owen-archetype-homologies-1848:
Richard Owen, Britain's leading anatomist, published his study of the vertebrate skeleton in 1848. Owen compared bones across fish, reptiles, birds, and mammals. He saw one hidden pattern beneath their many shapes.

Owen calls that pattern the archetype, an ideal plan of the backbone and skull. Bones that match across species, he names homologies, a term science still uses. His scheme came before Darwin and pointed to a rival cause, yet it framed the debate. Darwin later used Owen's own facts to argue for descent with change. His terms let anatomists compare skeletons across the whole animal kingdom.
plos-pone-0003448:
César Mattei and co-authors tested a natural compound against seafood poison in this 2008 study. Ciguatoxins come from tiny sea algae and build up in reef fish. They cause ciguatera, a nasty food poisoning of the nerves. A related compound, brevenal, was known to block a sister toxin.

The team used hormone-making cells from cattle for their tests. Pacific ciguatoxin-1B made those cells release far too much content. Brevenal curbed that toxin-driven release. The result hints at a treatment path for a poisoning that now has none. Ciguatera sickens many thousands of people in tropical regions each year.
plos-pone-0003548:
Maria A. Croyle and co-authors delivered a vaccine through the nose in this 2008 mouse study. Many people already have immunity to adenovirus type 5. That virus is a popular carrier for vaccine genes. Prior immunity can blunt a vaccine built on it.

The team compared muscle, nose, and oral delivery routes in mice. The vaccine expressed an Ebola surface protein for the tests. Nasal delivery bypassed the pre-existing immunity problem. It also improved the immune response over other routes. The nose route also avoids needles, which could help mass vaccine drives.
plos-pone-0003648:
Tomoyasu Wakuda, Hideo Matsuzaki, Katsuaki Suzuki, and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Lack of oxygen around birth is a suspected risk factor for schizophrenia later in life. The team used rats to test how such an oxygen loss affects the brain.

Pups that went through perinatal asphyxia grew fewer dentate granule cells, a type of neuron in the hippocampus. As adults, the same animals also showed stronger overactivity when given methamphetamine. The work supports the idea that a hard start at birth can leave lasting marks on the brain.
plos-pone-0003748:
Pedro José Barbosa Pereira, Nuno Empadinhas, Luciana Albuquerque, and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Tuberculosis remains a serious threat, worsened by drug-resistant strains of its bacterium. Few new compounds against it have been developed. The team solved the structure of one of its enzymes.

The enzyme builds a sugar needed for the bacterium's methylglucose lipopolysaccharides, a part of its outer chemistry. Knowing its atomic structure hands drug designers a concrete target. A drug that jams this key step could weaken Mycobacterium tuberculosis where current drugs fail.
plos-pone-0003848:
Rosana D. Meyer, David B. Sacks, and Nader Rahimi published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. VEGFR-2 is the main receptor for the growth factor that builds blood vessels. Its signaling is required for normal development and feeds pathological vessel growth in cancer and eye disease.

The team found a signaling pathway dependent on the scaffold protein IQGAP1. That pathway regulates endothelial cell proliferation and angiogenesis downstream of the receptor. plos-pone-0003948:

Parasites of the genus Eimeria cause the disease. A subunit vaccine was made from purified proteins of one species, Eimeria maxima.

Their PLOS ONE article reports use of that vaccine under field conditions. The vaccine aimed to prompt hens to pass protection to their chicks. Farm-level evidence matters more than lab results for poultry disease control. A working subunit vaccine could cut losses without heavy drug use. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004048:
Yves Gingras, Vincent Larivière, Benoît Macaluso, and co-authors measured how aging affects researchers in 2008. The average age of a first NIH grant in the U.S. rose over decades. It climbed from 34.3 years in 1970 to 41.7 in 2004. That trend raised questions about older scientists' output.

Their PLOS ONE article drew on a sizable sample of researchers. They tracked publication and citation patterns across career ages. Whether impact fades, holds, or grows with age matters for funding policy. Evidence can counter easy assumptions about aging and creativity. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004148:
Francesco Bonadonna, Samuel Caro, and M. de L. Brooke published this bird study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chemical signals can tell an animal another's identity, rank, or sex. Birds were long thought to barely use smell, yet recent work shows several species use chemical cues to find food and recognise each other.

The team asked whether Antarctic prions, seabirds that breed in burrows, can tell male from female by scent alone. Testing this sense in a wild seabird pushes against the old view of birds as poor smellers. Whatever the birds reveal, the study widens what we know about how animals read sex from smell.
plos-pone-0004248:
Nathaniel Sowa, Kunjumon Vadakkan, and Mark Zylka published this pain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prostatic acid phosphatase, or PAP, is made by pain-sensing neurons and works as an ectonucleotidase, an enzyme that processes nucleotides outside cells. Injected human and bovine PAP proteins produce strong, long-lasting pain relief that depends on A1-adenosine receptors.

The team made the mouse version of PAP in the lab and tested it. They report that its enzyme activity depends on pH and that it relieves pain through the same A1 receptors. The work supports PAP as a possible long-acting, non-opioid pain treatment.
plos-pone-0004348:

Customised zinc finger nucleases form the basis of a broadly applicable tool for highly efficient genome modification. They are artificial restriction enzymes: a non-specific nuclease domain fused to a zinc finger array engineered to recognise a chosen DNA sequence.

The team applied nucleases made by oligomerized pool engineering, called OPEN, to rapidly mutate endogenous zebrafish genes. Editing a fish's own genes in place, rather than adding copies, made the method practical. The study helped turn zinc finger editing into a routine laboratory tool.
plos-pone-0004448: In 2009, Lu, Zhang, and Wu told two ancient grains apart. Phytolith analysis cleanly distinguished foxtail millet from common millet. The tiny silica skeletons separated the two crops. The neat method aids crop archaeology. The millets are Eurasia's oldest dry-farmed crops.
plos-pone-0004548: In 2009, van Veen, McNamee, and Richardus weighed leprosy disability programs' value anew. Cost-effectiveness of interventions to prevent disability in leprosy was reviewed. plos-pone-0004648: In 2009, Biocca, Falconi, and Filesi ran computer trials of a cholesterol sensor variant. Computer trials of LOX-1 K167N showed changed behavior. plos-pone-0004748: In 2009, Alberts built a virtual cell bending its rods anew here today. The fake cell's rods bent like real ones today. The simple bits made lifelike motion anew. The tool aids cell research well. The tiny hookups are molecular indeed here.
early-travels-palestine-wright-1848:
Pilgrims' tales of the Holy Land crowd Early Travels in Palestine, edited by Thomas Wright in 1848. Arculf in the 600s and Willibald in the 700s lead the company. Bernard, Saewulf, and Sigurd the Crusader add their own reports of the road.

Each traveler describes Jerusalem and Bethlehem as he found them. Shrines, dangers, and wonders crowd their brisk, credulous pages. Wright gathered the texts for Bohn's Library of standard works. The book lets the Middle Ages report from the ground. Its voices are raw and earnest, and it stays a handy door into the age of pilgrimage.
ashburner-facts-clairvoyance-zoist-1848:
John Ashburner gathered cases of clairvoyance from the journal Zoist in 1848, under the title Facts in Clairvoyance. Subjects in the magnetic trance, witnesses swore, described far-off scenes correctly. Others named hidden objects or read sealed letters without the use of their eyes at all.

Ashburner, a London doctor and keen mesmerist, presents the tales as evidence. Victorian believers treated the file as proof of unseen powers. Skeptics then and now read the same pages very differently indeed. Either way, the book stands as a key primary source for the history of the paranormal in Britain.
euler-introductio-analysin-1748:
Euler founds analysis as its own field in his Introductio in analysin infinitorum, in Latin from 1748. Functions take their modern form in its opening chapters here. Endless series unfold, and the number e gains the notation and treatment that students still learn from textbooks today across the world.

Many call this the book where modern mathematics truly begins. Euler writes the grammar of a new science with unmatched fertility of mind. Curves, logs, and trig functions all fall into one grand order. The most fertile mind of his age speaks here at full stretch, and the echo of his choices still shapes every page of higher math.
seneca-falls-declaration-1848:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton and her allies adopted the Declaration of Sentiments in 1848. The Seneca Falls meeting launched the fight for women's rights. Stanton took the Declaration of Independence as her direct model.

All men and women are created equal, her bold rewrite declares. A list of grievances then charges men with a long tyranny. Denied votes, wages, schooling, and legal standing fill the counts. The call for the ballot shocked even many friends of reform. American feminism counts this short text as its founding manifesto to this day. Its grievance list reads like a mirror held up to 1776 itself.
truman-eo-9981-1948:
Harry S. Truman signed Executive Order 9981 in 1948, by his own hand. The order demands fair treatment for all in the armed forces. Race, color, faith, or origin shall not bar a soldier's fair chance.

Segregation in uniform was to end under the order's firm terms. Truman acted over his generals' doubts and the South's loud anger. The order changed the American military more deeply than any since. Black troops gained a legal claim their service had long earned. Between Lincoln and Johnson, no president struck a bolder rights blow alone. Full integration took years, but the order made it the law's clear aim.
treaty-of-guadalupe-hidalgo-1848:
The treaty that ended the Mexican-American War was signed in 1848 at Guadalupe Hidalgo, near Mexico City. Defeated in war, Mexico gave up a vast share of its northern territory to the United States. The land included California and much of what became Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, and Colorado.

In return, the United States paid Mexico fifteen million dollars and took on some claims owed to American citizens. The Rio Grande became the border for Texas, and Mexicans living in the ceded lands could choose which country to join. The treaty completed the map of the continental United States, but it left a lasting wound in Mexican memory.
udhr-1948:
The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in Paris in December 1948. Eleanor Roosevelt led the committee that drafted it, drawing on traditions from many countries. The declaration came in the shadow of the Second World War and the Holocaust, when the world had seen where contempt for human rights could lead.

Its thirty articles proclaim rights held by every person, including free speech, fair trials, education, and freedom of religion. The declaration is not a treaty and binds no court, yet it has guided laws and constitutions across the globe. It remains the foundation stone of modern human rights work and the most translated document in history.
french-constitution-1848:
France wrote a new constitution in 1848 after the February Revolution toppled King Louis-Philippe. The charter founded the Second Republic in the springtime of the peoples, when thrones shook across Europe. Its makers tried to join a strong executive to the widest democracy France had known.

The text grants the vote to all adult men, the first full manhood suffrage in French history. It creates a president elected by the people for four years, facing a single elected assembly. In December 1848 the voters chose Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte as president. Within four years he seized full power in a coup and strangled the republic his office came from. The constitution remains the charter of 1848's hope and of its winter, the republic that elected its own destroyer.

Abduction plots forced embassies and consulates to weigh guards, routes, and daily habits. Most warnings never became public, and many plots never came off. plos-pone-0010448: Many gay men in Peru don't know their HIV status but live online. This randomized trial tests whether web videos can nudge them toward testing. The paper evaluates the internet as a public-health outreach tool. The trial tests whether a screen can succeed where clinics struggle.
plos-pone-0010548: Hearts beat electrically — but stretching the muscle also changes the electricity. This study investigates mechano-electric feedback in fish hearts. The paper extends a cardiac principle to a new vertebrate class. The work shows heart physics conserved across vertebrates, from fish to mammals.
plos-pone-0010648: A brain-size gene variant common today may have Neanderthal roots. This study finds the ancestral microcephalin allele in a Neanderthal individual. The paper adds a chapter to human brain evolution. The allele links our brains to our extinct cousins.
plos-pone-0010748: A tiny RNA can fight brain cancer. This study shows microRNA-128a raises ROS by targeting Bmi-1, pushing medulloblastoma cells into senescence. The paper reveals a tumor-suppressing RNA. The mechanism suggests a new therapy for this childhood brain cancer.
plos-pone-0010848: Neurons are long-haul shippers of mitochondria. This study shows the enzyme HDAC6 controls mitochondrial transport along microtubules in hippocampal neurons. The paper reveals the traffic controller. The finding matters for Alzheimer's and other brain diseases. The controller keeps the cell's power grid moving.
plos-pone-0010948: A fish's immune genes shift as populations split. This study compares immune-gene differences in sticklebacks that live side by side versus far apart. The paper probes how new species form. The finding catches evolution in the act. The genes mirror the fish's diverging worlds.
plos-pone-0011048: Gene chips work through the chemistry of DNA binding. This study applies equilibrium models of solution hybridization to microarray probe design and analysis. The paper makes probe behavior predictable. The method sharpens genomic experiments. The models tame probe-design guesswork.
plos-pone-0011148: A spit test could catch mouth cancer early. This proteomics study finds myosin and actin in saliva can distinguish pre-malignant from malignant oral lesions. The paper offers a noninvasive diagnostic. The finding could boost oral-cancer survival. The boost comes from earlier treatment.
plos-pone-0011248: Two small fish swim in step when they see the same motion. This study gets a pair of fish moving as one by showing them matching moving stripes. The paper reveals schooling's building blocks. The finding aids behavior work. The blocks explain how schools form.
plos-pone-0011348: Why do some mice resist allergic asthma while others suffer? This study models susceptibility versus resistance in allergic airway disease, revealing regulation by the Tec kinase Itk. The paper offers a disease model. The finding aids asthma research. The aided research hunts new asthma drugs.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1248:
President Truman wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on 25 July 1945. The two men exchanged notes through the whole Churchill week at Potsdam. This one came on the prime minister's last full day at the talks.

The count in London the next day would end Churchill's leadership. Neither man wrote as if the partnership were ending; the work went on to the final hour. This message belongs to that last day of joint business. It is part of the closing set of letters between the president and the prime minister who had led Britain through the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1348:
The acting secretary of state sent instructions to John Winant, the American ambassador in London, on 16 July 1945. That was the day before the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945 formally opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

London was Washington's closest partner and its first sounding board in 1945. Instructions sent on the eve of a summit set the line an ambassador should hold with the host government. Readers can use this message to see what Washington wanted London to know. To do. As Truman and Byrnes set out for Germany and the talks with Stalin began.
frus-1945-50-intel-d48:
Minutes of the 168th meeting of the Secretary of State's Staff Committee are dated 20 November 1945. The numbered meetings show a standing body grinding through the department's business week by week. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A numbered run of minutes lets readers watch an institution think over time. The 168th meeting took up the department's affairs with the intelligence question at its height. What the committee agreed, deferred, or sent upward shaped the State Department's final position. The volume prints several of these committee records. Together they give the State side of the story an official spine that the letters alone would lack.
frus-1945-50-intel-d148: On 29 April 1946, the Director of Central Intelligence (Souers) put a memorandum into the files. It is document 148 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff. Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings.
frus-1945-50-intel-d248:
A memorandum from the Deputy Director (Wright) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 4 November 1947. It stands as document 248 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d348:
Formal minutes cover a meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Committee, held on 16 June 1948. It is document 348 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1861-d48:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 31 May 1861. The dispatch is document 48 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Britain had now declared its neutrality and granted the South the rights of a belligerent. Adams had to accept that step while blocking any move beyond it. His end of May report shows the care with which he drew that line in talk with British ministers. Adams treated the belligerent grant as a fixed fact and fought on the ground beyond it. Beyond that line lay recognition, and on that line Adams would not yield an inch.
frus-1861-d148:
On 22 August 1861, William Dayton sent a further report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 148 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late August found Dayton watching French yards and ports for Southern orders. Confederate buyers sought ships and arms where they could. His report belongs to the quiet counter work that kept such goods from sailing under French colors. Southern buyers in France worked through banks and brokers, hard men to track. Hard men to track were tracked all the same, by consuls, clerks, and patience. Tracked all the same, by patience and proof.
frus-1861-d248:
James Shepherd Pike reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 18 August 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 248 in the President's message volume for 1861. It was written in the first summer of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d48:
16 April 1862 is stamped on a letter Seward got from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The printed record keeps it as Document 48 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. The date falls in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d148:
Dated 22 September 1862, Document 148 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It forms one link in the long chain of orders and reports that bound Washington to its legation in Britain during the Civil War.

On that same date Lincoln issued his first Emancipation Proclamation, warning that enslaved people in rebel states would be freed on 1 January. The step changed what the war was about in foreign eyes. Seward's mail to London in these days went out as that news began its slow trip across the sea.
frus-1862-d248:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, sent William L. Dayton a dispatch on 2 January 1862, printed as Document 248 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris, the Union's voice at the court of Napoleon III.

The new year opened with French, British, and Spanish forces gathering in Mexico, a move Washington watched with deep distrust. Dayton's standing task was to defend Union interests without pushing France toward the Confederacy. Seward's January letters set his envoy's line for a year in which Mexico and the war would stay tightly linked. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d348:
Document 348 opens the file of France's minister in Washington: a letter dated 7 December 1861 from Henri Mercier to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The catalog title spells his name Merrier. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier represented Napoleon III's France in the Union capital, a post of great delicacy during the Civil War. December 1861 was the Trent crisis month, and every foreign envoy in Washington watched the Anglo-American quarrel closely. Mercier's letters to Seward form the French counterpart to the British file in this volume. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d448:
Baron Friedrich von Gerolt, the Prussian minister in Washington, received this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 May 1861. It is Document 448 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, one of its earliest papers.

Gerolt was the dean of Washington's diplomatic corps, long resident and deeply read in American affairs. In May 1861 the war was a month old, and Seward was setting the terms on which foreign governments would deal with the rebellion. A note to Prussia's minister in those weeks belonged to the first framing of the Union's case. The case ran: one nation, a domestic revolt, no foreign hand welcome. The letter reaches back to the spring when all the volume's later files began.
frus-1862-d548:
Dated 27 September 1862, this note from Roest van Limburg to Secretary of State William H. Seward was printed after its successor in the volume's Dutch file. It is Document 548 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The slight disorder of dates is a window on how the volume was made. Papers were gathered by subject. They were printed as the files came together, not in perfect time order. Van Limburg's late-September note dealt with the standing questions between his government and the United States. Read with the note of 29 September, it shows the Dutch legation working steadily through the autumn. Meanwhile Antietam and emancipation remade the setting. All Washington diplomacy was done in that new setting.
frus-1862-d648:
Robert H. Pruyn, the American minister to Japan, dated this dispatch 15 May 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 648 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed among the papers on Japan. Pruyn had stepped into the job only weeks before.

Ministers abroad wrote on a set rhythm, sending news, requests, and accounts of their talks with local rulers. Pruyn's letter is part of that steady flow from the Japan legation. For readers today, it shows American ties with Japan in their first years. A handful of men ran them, writing letters that took months to cross the Pacific.
frus-1863p1-d48:
On 25 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to James M. Mason for the second day in a row. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 48 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Back-to-back letters from a treasury chief point to deals that would not wait. The South's credit in Europe hung on cotton and on faith that the new republic would last. Memminger's sheets to Mason fed that work. With its twin, this letter shows Richmond's money men writing in haste in the fall of 1862, as costs rose and the purse shrank.
frus-1863p1-d148:
In a week the ship news ran the Union's way, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 8 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London, and a dispatch from him sits just before this letter in the volume. The letter is document 148 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's April letters kept the press on while the ship news ran the Union's way. He had to hold the gains without crowing, since Britain's pride was a force of its own. This letter is Washington's word in a same-week cross with London. It shows the secretary's care with tone, the skill that matched Adams's own and made the pair so strong.
frus-1863p1-d248:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 24 July 1863. The letter is document 248 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d348:
Washington's business with Britain on 31 December 1862 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 348 of the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Notes on this route often dealt with single ships, single cargoes, or single men. Small cases mattered, because each one tested what neutrality would allow. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d448:
A letter of 6 April 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 448 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d548:
In the flow of wartime mail, F. W. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 3 June 1863. F. W. Seward was the Assistant Secretary of State, writing here to Britain's minister in Washington. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them.
frus-1863p1-d648:
The 26 October 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020248:
Robert L. Hammond and Laurent Keller reviewed a conflict inside insect societies in PLOS Biology in 2004. In ant, bee, and wasp colonies, workers are often related more to some males than to others. That skew creates conflict over which males get raised and whose sons the queen's mates produce.

Theory predicts workers should favor their closest kin, yet colonies mostly run smoothly. The authors weigh how workers police each other and how queens limit strife. Their review sorts strong evidence from neat but untested ideas. Social insects are a test bed for the whole theory of cooperation. A clear account of their one big conflict sharpens that theory.
plos-pone-0000148:
Chunyi Li, Jo-Ann L. Stanton, Tracy M. Robertson, and colleagues published this deer biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Red deer regrow their antlers every year, one of the fastest examples of organ regeneration in mammals. The authors measured nerve growth factor messages in the regenerating antler tip of Cervus elaphus.

Nerves must regrow along with bone and skin for a new antler to form. Tracking where and when nerve growth factor is expressed shows how that regrowth is guided. Antlers are a prized natural model of regeneration, so findings here interest biologists who study how tissues rebuild themselves.
plos-pone-0000248:
Jonathan S. Friedlaender, Françoise R. Friedlaender, Jason A. Hodgson, and colleagues published this population genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It studies the mitochondrial DNA of Melanesian peoples, the populations of the Pacific islands northeast of Australia. The title flags the theme: their mtDNA shows striking complexity.

Melanesia was settled in layers over tens of thousands of years, and its DNA carries that history. The authors untangle patterns of maternal lineages across the region. The work helps reconstruct how humans spread through the Pacific, one of the last great chapters of human migration.
plos-pone-0000348:
David Lusseau published this dolphin behavior paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. In the bottlenose dolphin population of Doubtful Sound, New Zealand, male social relationships are unusually complex. The author asks why, examining the social network of males in this isolated fjord population.

Male dolphins elsewhere form alliances with clear tiers; Doubtful Sound's pattern differs. Working out what drives that difference tests general theories of animal society. The study uses long-term observation of known individuals, the strength of this small, well-watched population. Doubtful Sound's isolation makes it a natural test case, since what holds there may not match busier coasts.
plos-pone-0000448:
Philippe Boucher and colleagues described a blood vessel protein that gathers growth signals, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The protein, LRP1, functions as an atheroprotective integrator. It helps protect arteries from the plaque buildup of atherosclerosis. It does this by combining signals from TGFβ and PDGF, two growth factors in the vascular wall.

The team drew out implications for Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder that weakens the aorta. A protein that both reads growth signals and guards the vessel wall sits at a crossroads of several diseases. Work of this kind helps explain how one signaling fault can produce widespread damage in arteries.
plos-pone-0000548:
Yang Liu and colleagues solved the structure of a fish antifreeze and traced its origin, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Herring survive icy water with a type II antifreeze protein that stops ice crystals from growing, and the protein needs calcium ions to work. The team determined the structure and evolutionary origin of this Ca2+-dependent protein.

Antifreeze proteins evolved several times independently, making them a natural experiment in invention. A structure shows exactly how the protein grips ice, and its ancestry shows which ordinary protein was reshaped into antifreeze. Both views matter for designing synthetic antifreezes for medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0000648:
Todd A. Sangster, Adam Bahrami, Amity Wilczek and co-authors lowered a protective protein in Arabidopsis plants and watched the variety that emerged. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study concerns HSP90, a molecular chaperone that helps select proteins mature correctly. Many of its client proteins sit in key signal pathways. Its role had been studied mostly in animals and fungi.

With reduced HSP90, the plants showed wider phenotypic diversity, a broader spread of visible traits. Their ability to adjust to the environment changed too. The result supports the idea that HSP90 buffers hidden genetic variation, letting it surface when the chaperone weakens. Evolution researchers prize such mechanisms for explaining sudden trait changes.
plos-pone-0000748:
Martin Weinberger, Li Feng, Anita Paul and colleagues tied the stress of copying DNA to how long yeast cells live, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Chronological lifespan in budding yeast means how long non-dividing cells survive. Mutations that switch off conserved growth-signaling pathways extend that lifespan. Those pathways regulate entry into and progress through the cell cycle.

The authors show that DNA replication stress is a determinant of this lifespan. Copying damage accumulated earlier seems to set a clock on later survival. Aging research prizes such links, because growth pathways and replication stress also appear in human aging and cancer. Yeast offers the fast, cheap system for testing them.
plos-pone-0000848:
Basilis Zikopoulos and Helen Barbas mapped two kinds of wiring between the brain's executive region and its relay station, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pathways linking the thalamus and cortex mediate our daily shifts from attention to quiet rest or sleep. Little was known about their architecture in high-order systems tied to cognition, emotion, and action. The prefrontal cortex is the seat of those high-order functions.

The authors provide novel neurochemical evidence for parallel driving and modulatory pathways linking prefrontal cortex and thalamus. Driving pathways carry the main message; modulatory ones tune it. That division, proven for sensory systems, apparently extends to the circuits of thought itself.
plos-pone-0000948:
Gerald Lim, Greg Huber, Yoshihiro Torii and colleagues modeled the fission yeast nucleus as if it were a tiny fluid sac, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Fission yeast divides with its nuclear envelope intact. During that closed division, the nucleus stretches through a striking series of shapes as the spindle inside it grows.

The authors argue that vesicle like mechanics, the physics of a soft membrane sac, govern much of that geometry. Treating the nucleus as a physical object, not just a bag of genes, explains shapes that pure biology leaves puzzling. The approach links cell biology with soft matter physics in a testable way.
plos-pone-0001048:
Christopher Smith, Michael Gill, Janet May and colleagues showed how a mouse herpesvirus hides from dendritic cells, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dendritic cells start adaptive immune responses, so viruses that infect them gain a strong advantage. Murine gammaherpesvirus-68 infects dendritic cells during normal colonization of its host.

The team report the virus inhibits antigen presentation by those cells, weakening the alarm they should raise. A virus that mutes its host's sentries can persist for life, as herpesviruses do. Studying the trick in a mouse virus reveals principles that apply to human relatives, including ones tied to cancer.
plos-pone-0001148:
Flaxseed has been shown to improve blood lipids in people, and a flaxseed compound called lignan improved blood sugar control in animals. An Pan and colleagues put the lignan to a human test in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their trial involved patients with type 2 diabetes.

The study was randomized, double-blind, and used a cross-over design, so each patient served as their own comparison. It measured the supplement's effects on blood sugar control, lipid profiles, and insulin measures. The paper adds controlled human evidence to a question mostly studied in animals before.
plos-pone-0001248:
Soil ecology has produced a huge body of results on soil organisms and the processes they control. Sébastien Barot, Manuel Blouin, and Sébastien Fontaine argue that the field still lacks theory tying those results together, in a 2007 PLOS ONE essay. They frame the problem as a tale of four stories: soil ecology, theory, evolution, and the publication system.

Some soil scientists think the field is short of modeling and evolutionary thinking, the authors note. Their essay examines why, including how publishing incentives reward description over synthesis. It is an opinion and analysis piece aimed at the field's habits as much as its data.
plos-pone-0001348:
Thymopentin, or TP5, is a small peptide used to stimulate the immune system by contacting T cells. Zuojia Liu and colleagues modeled how it binds to HLA-DR molecules, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The molecular basis of how TP5 achieves its immune triggering remained incompletely understood.

HLA-DR molecules present peptide fragments to T cells, so a TP5 complex with them is a plausible trigger mechanism. The authors carry out a molecular analysis of that binding. Understanding the complex could guide the design of peptide immunomodulators with more predictable effects.
plos-pone-0001448:
Craig Bennett and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study that used yeast to find partners of a breast cancer gene. The gene, BRCA1, is tied to many DNA repair paths that keep the genome sound. Which of its jobs stops tumors was still obscure. The team screened yeast for the most kept, core links of BRCA1.

Their screen flagged the tail of the main gene copying enzyme and a partner factor as key targets. Yeast and human cells share these core parts. Hits that survive that long span of evolution are likely central. The work helps narrow a wide field to the BRCA1 jobs that matter most.
plos-pone-0001548:
Stuart Sandin and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on coral reefs in the Northern Line Islands. Good guard work needs a true picture of a reef left alone. Most reefs are worn down by fishing, waste, and other human acts. The team surveyed reefs that range from near pristine to heavily used.

Their data set a base line for what a sound reef holds in fish, coral, and microbes. Reefs near people show clear drops from that base. A firm base line lets managers judge if guard steps work. It also shows what is lost, step by step, as use grows.
plos-pone-0001648:
Kathryn L. Lipson, Rajarshi Ghosh, and Fumihiko Urano studied stress inside insulin-making cells for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Insulin is built in the endoplasmic reticulum, a cell compartment where new secretory proteins are folded. When folding goes wrong, the cell feels ER stress and switches on a set of rescue pathways called the unfolded protein response.

The team focused on IRE1α, one sensor of that stress, in pancreatic beta cells. Their work shows this sensor plays a part in breaking down insulin's gene message when stress hits. The full text gives the cell tests and message levels they measured. The finding links ER stress to falling insulin output, a core fault in diabetes, and names a protein that future drug work may target.
plos-pone-0001748:
James T. Mandel, John M. Ratcliffe, David J. Cerasale, and their co-authors tested side preferences in flying swallows in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Many vertebrates favor one side of the body, a result of brain hemispheric specialization. Side bias can speed responses and help multitasking, but it can also bend body shape into asymmetries.

The team ran concurrent tests of side bias and optimality in flying tree swallows. They asked whether the birds favor a side, and whether that side is the better one for flight tasks. The full text gives the flight tests and the turning data. Swallows feed on the wing at high speed, so their choices test how lateralization works under real aerodynamic pressure.
plos-pone-0001848:
Matthias Vömel and Christian Wegener mapped amine signaling systems in the fruit fly larva's nerve cord in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Biogenic amines are important signaling molecules in the central nervous systems of vertebrates and invertebrates alike. In Drosophila melanogaster, amines help regulate feeding, learning and memory, and other vital processes.

Their paper gives the neuroarchitecture of aminergic systems in the larval ventral ganglion: which neurons make each amine and where their fibers run. The full text gives the staining maps cell by cell. A wiring atlas of the larva's amine systems is reference material for the many labs that use fly larvae to study behavior genetics.
plos-pone-0001948:
Klaus Stark and co-authors tested a gene's link to two ills at once, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The gene, GLUT9, moves uric acid in the body. Two large genome scans had tied common forms of it to uric acid levels in Italian and British groups. High uric acid is the cause of gout and often comes with metabolic syndrome.

In a large case and control study, the team asked whether those same gene forms track with gout. They also asked about coronary artery disease, a heart illness. As the title states, they found a link to gout but not to heart disease. Such splits help sort cause from mere company.
plos-pone-0002048:
Michael Bryan and co-authors traced a gene that jumps between sea viruses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. S-PM2 is a virus that infects Synechococcus, a one-celled cyanobacterium common in the oceans. Like kin viruses, it carries genes that look bacterial, picked up from hosts at some point in its past.

One such gene makes a MazG-like protein, present in high copy. As the title states, the evidence points to intense exchange of MazG among marine cyanophages. The route is horizontal gene transfer, genes passed sideways rather than from parent to offspring. Sea viruses, it seems, trade tools freely.
plos-pone-0002148:
Roberto Galán studied the patterns that brain circuits produce on their own, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Even with no sensory input, networks in the neocortex, the brain's outer sheet, fire in complex patterns. These patterns are thought to reflect how the network is built, including how it is divided into modules.

Galán asked how the layout of connections shapes which patterns take over. His work connects wiring to activity: the same neurons can settle into different dominant rhythms depending on how they are linked. That link helps explain how a resting brain can hold ready-made patterns for thought and action.
plos-pone-0002248:
Yusuke Ohnishi and co-authors improved a way to silence one faulty gene copy while sparing the healthy one, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Many diseases come from a single bad allele, one copy of a gene, while its twin copy is normal. RNA interference can silence genes, and allele-specific silencing aims to hit only the bad copy.

The team found that adding deliberate single-letter mismatches to the silencing RNA sharpens the contrast between copies. That makes the treatment cut the disease allele's output while leaving the normal allele closer to untouched. Finer control like this is vital if RNA drugs are to be safe.
plos-pone-0002348:
Eric Mooshagian, Jonas Kaplan, and Eran Zaidel studied how fast the brain answers when a stimulus appears twice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Processing several stimuli in parallel is critical for dealing with a busy world. One test of that ability measures reaction times to redundant targets, multiple copies of the same stimulus, which people answer faster than to one.

The team asked what role the right temporo-parietal junction, a region where the temporal and parietal lobes meet, plays in that speed-up. Their results tie this brain hub to fast visuomotor processing of redundant targets. The finding helps explain how the brain turns several signals into one quick action.
plos-pone-0002448:
Siroux and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Valérie Siroux, Emmanuelle Bouzigon, Marie-Hélène Dizier, and others. Its subject is replication of Association between ADAM33 Polymorphisms and Psoriasis. Polymorphisms in ADAM33, the first gene identified in asthma by positional cloning, have been recently linked to psoriasis.

No replication study of this association has been published so far. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002548:
Led by Gu, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Peili Gu, Jeffrey G. Reid, Xiaolian Gao, and others.
